opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's an interesting part of my story, because I actually had a failed start before AlexNet.

As an undergrad in Shanghai, I was already playing with neural networks. I remember writing GPU code for things like restricted Boltzmann machines and early convolutional nets. It was exciting, but honestly the results weren't great. The models didn't beat the more traditional methods we were comparing against, and at some point I asked myself whether I was spending a lot of effort on something that just didn't work. So I stepped away from it and moved toward things like tree boosting and large-scale machine learning. That direction later became XGBoost.

Then AlexNet came out in 2012, and it was a real shock. Here was a deep convolutional network trained on GPUs, beating everything else on ImageNet by a big margin. My first reaction was a bit of regret. I thought, "Wait, I was working on almost exactly this kind of thing, and I gave up." But the bigger feeling was that the door had reopened. It showed that the ideas weren't wrong. The missing pieces were scale, data, and engineering, making it possible to actually train these models efficiently.

That gave me the confidence to go back and build tools again. Some of us started writing our own GPU-based deep learning code. That became something called CXXNet, and later we joined with other groups to build MXNet. What changed for me was realizing that systems work wasn't a side detail. If you build the right abstractions and make things fast and flexible, you let many more people try ideas that would otherwise be too painful to try.

So AlexNet was a turning point in two ways. It showed that deep learning really could work, and it convinced me that building the infrastructure underneath it was worth investing in. That way of thinking, connecting machine learning with systems, has shaped pretty much everything I've done since.

r001.rationale: The response says CXXNet grew from GPU-based deep learning code, but does not mention expression templates or fusing update-rule arithmetic into a single inlined GPU kernel.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it changed everything for me. Before AlexNet, I had actually spent a lot of time trying to build a deep learning system — this was around 2010, 2011, back in undergrad. I was working on things like restricted Boltzmann machines, convolutional nets on GPUs, and I wrote a lot of code to get that running. And the results were just... not that exciting. We'd get something that worked, but it wasn't dramatically better than what you could get with simpler methods, and the whole experience was quite painful. The training was slow, the tooling was almost nonexistent, and it felt like you were pouring a huge amount of engineering effort into something where the payoff wasn't clear. So I kind of gave up on it, to be honest. I moved on to other things — tree boosting, which later became XGBoost, and more traditional machine learning.

Then AlexNet came out in 2012, and it was a very different feeling. Suddenly you had this clear demonstration that if you scale things up, if you use GPUs properly, if you get the data and the architecture right, the model just wins by a large margin. It wasn't a marginal improvement; it was a step change. And that reframed the question for me. It was no longer "does deep learning work?" — it was "how do we make it easy for people to do this?"

So the engineering pain I had experienced earlier stopped being a reason to walk away and started being the actual problem worth solving. All that effort I'd put in before — writing GPU kernels, figuring out how to lay out memory, how to express these computations — turned out to be useful knowledge, just applied in the wrong moment. And that's really what motivated going back and thinking about frameworks seriously, which eventually led to things like CXXNet and later MXNet. The lesson I took was that sometimes the idea isn't wrong, the timing is. You just need the evidence that the direction is real before it makes sense to invest in building infrastructure for it.

astra-6.text: AlexNet made me feel that deep learning was really working—that there was a reason to try again. Before that, it was harder to know whether the effort of building a framework would pay off. Seeing that success gave me more confidence that these models were going to be useful, and that better software could help more people experiment with them. So I became much more willing to put time into building a framework again.
